opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about more than I'd like to admit.

I think the first thing I had to accept is that holding a value firmly doesn't mean the world owes me agreement. Early on, when I saw something happen that I thought was clearly wrong, whether in how technology gets built, how people get treated, or how decisions get made, my instinct was frustration, almost disbelief. Like, how can this still be happening? Over time I realized that disbelief isn't very useful. It just drains energy.

So I try to separate two things: what I believe should be true, and what I can actually influence. The values don't change. I don't lower my standard because the world isn't meeting it. But I get more practical about where I put my effort. I ask: what's within my reach? Can I build something that makes the better path easier? Can I make a tool open so more people have access to it? Can I treat the people I work with the way I think people should be treated, even if that's not the norm around me?

I've also found that building is my way of coping. In engineering and research, if you don't like how something works, you can often go make an alternative and let it speak for itself. That's much more satisfying to me than arguing. And when it works, when other people pick it up and use it, you realize you've shifted things a little, even if you didn't change everything.

The other part is patience. A lot of things I believe in happen slowly, not on the timescale I'd want. So I try to think in terms of years, not weeks. If I keep acting consistently with what I believe, and I find others who share those values, the direction can change, even if every single day it looks like nothing is moving.

So I don't really reconcile it in the sense of making peace with it. I'd say I've learned to live with the tension, and to use it as motivation rather than letting it turn into cynicism.

r001.rationale: The response separates frustration and disbelief about events from her underlying values, which she says do not change.

r002.rationale: She says she does not lower her standard when the world falls short and has not made peace with the unwanted events.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that people need positive feedback before they can be expected to persist in their convictions.

r004.rationale: She describes patience and thinking in years, but does not attribute that increased willingness to wait to repeated eventual validation.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've sat with for a long time, honestly, because for most of my life I thought the answer was that you just hold on tighter. If something shouldn't happen and it keeps happening, then clearly the world is wrong and I need to push harder. And I did that for years. It works, sometimes. But it also burns you out, and it makes you a little self-righteous, which is its own kind of blindness.

What changed for me was realizing that there's a difference between a value and a prediction. A value is "I believe people should be treated fairly," or "I believe work should be done honestly, with credit going where it's due." A prediction is "therefore this will happen." I had been quietly fusing those two things together, so every time the world violated the value, it felt like it was also disproving me. And that's exhausting, because the world is going to violate your values a lot. That's not a bug in the world, that's just what it means to have values that are more demanding than the status quo.

So the reconciliation, for me, isn't really a reconciliation. I don't think you're supposed to make peace with it. I think you hold the value, you accept that reality is going to keep disappointing you, and you ask a narrower question: given that, what can I actually do with the hands I have? In research, that meant I stopped waiting for the field to become the kind of place I wished it was and just tried to run my own corner that way. How I treat students, how I write up results, who I give credit to. It's a small radius. But the small radius is real, and the big complaint is mostly just noise in my own head.

The other thing I'd say is that the gap between what should be and what is, is actually the only reason to do anything. If the world already matched your values, you'd have nothing to work on. So on a good day, I can look at the stuff that keeps happening that shouldn't, and instead of feeling defeated, I can think, okay, that's the job. It's not always a good day. But that framing has kept me going longer than outrage ever did.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes values from predictions and describes distress, but does not distinguish emotional distress from how Ying Sheng’s values are formed.

r002.rationale: It says she does not think one should make peace with events that violate one’s values, and that she continues to hold those values.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss expecting everyone to persist in their convictions or the need for positive feedback.

r004.rationale: It does not say that repeated validation has made Ying Sheng more willing to wait for her convictions to be vindicated.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate what you believe should happen from what you expect will happen. Holding a value doesn’t mean the world has agreed to follow it. And when reality contradicts that value, it doesn’t automatically mean the value is wrong.

But it does mean you have something to examine. Am I misunderstanding the situation? Are my assumptions wrong? Or is this something I really do need to push back against? I want to be open to changing my understanding without letting every disappointment change what I stand for.

Then the question becomes: What can I actually do? Maybe I can’t prevent something from happening everywhere, but I can decide whether I contribute to it, whether I speak up, and how I treat the people around me. That doesn’t resolve the whole tension. I think you live with some of it. But it gives your values a practical role, beyond being a reason to feel disappointed in the world.

r001.rationale: The response separates values from expectations about the world, but does not distinguish emotional distress from how Ying Sheng constructs her values.

r002.rationale: It says that reality contradicting a value does not mean the value is wrong and considers whether to push back, conveying that witnessing an unwanted event does not make it acceptable.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss expecting others to persist in their convictions or positive feedback.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe repeated validation or how it affects the time Ying Sheng is willing to wait for vindication.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to separate what I believe should happen from what I expect will happen. My values tell me what I want to work toward; they don’t guarantee that the world will cooperate.

When something happens that I think is wrong, I try to ask: Is this challenging my values, or is it challenging my understanding of how the world works? Sometimes I need to revise my assumptions. Sometimes I need to speak up or change what I’m doing. And sometimes I have very little control, which is difficult to accept.

For me, reconciliation doesn’t mean becoming comfortable with everything that happens. It means being able to see reality clearly and still choose how to act. I can’t make the whole world consistent with my values, but I can try to make my own decisions consistent with them—and stay open to the possibility that I have something to learn.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes values from expectations, but does not distinguish emotional distress at events from how Ying Sheng constructs her values.

r002.rationale: She says reconciliation does not mean becoming comfortable with everything that happens, communicating that unwanted events do not become acceptable to her.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss expecting everyone to maintain convictions without positive feedback.

r004.rationale: The response does not say that repeated eventual validation has made Ying Sheng more willing to wait for her convictions to be vindicated.
